translation: The boundless sound of the sea did not cease for a minute.
Waves ran long, and alternately intensified and diminished.
The wind rustled in the bare trees, then fell silent, like me, listening to the flow of the night.
But it didn't leave, it was still here.
I knew by the smell of wet pebbles and barely audible trembling of a single plane tree leaf.
I noticed this stubborn grey leaf during daytime but now at night it seemed to be a small living creature, my only awake friend.
Occasionally from darkness outside in town rang out rifle shots; after each shot dogs barked for an extended period before becoming quiet.
Then in faraway sea flashed dull light that then faded away quickly.
He made us look at these things more closely and for longer than we usually do, thus revealing many qualities in them that had previously gone unnoticed.
In the porous yellow stone, there were many small seashells firmly embedded within it; on the broom shrubs a few more flowers remained.
They sat on straight solid stems like soaked and crumpled golden butterflies, patiently waiting for the sun.
However, it rarely broke through the fog as a blurred white spot and didn't provide either warmth or shadow.
Underneath the solitary old plane tree with lemon spots on its bark, leaves were strewn about as if cut out from dull green velvet.
Ants ran in a line through an iron gate, carrying their last reserve supplies underground for winter while under an anchor chain, a small timid toad made its home.
During the night, someone on the other side of the river started to wave a lantern and shout elongatedly.
Uncle Ilko and I went out to the bank.
The river was roaring.
Water cascaded down from the dam in a cold waterfall.
The late, deep night stood still without a single star overhead.
A wild freshness blowing from overflowing water and thawed earth touched our faces.
All this while someone was waving a lantern across the river and yelling, but their words were undecipherable over all noise of rushing water.
When the coffin was carried out onto the porch, I saw on the opposite side of the river an old carriage, horses unhitched and tethered to it, and a small woman in black mother.
She stood motionless on the shore.
From there she watched as they took father away.
Then she dropped to her knees and buried her head in the sand.
No, the grandfather replied.
It's true, they didn't see each other again.
Ostap started going blind.
He decided to walk to St. Petersburg in order to see that woman before he went completely blind.
When he reached the Tsar's capital city, he learned that she had died; perhaps she did not endure their separation.
Ostap found her white marble tombstone in a cemetery, looked at it and his heart broke; on the stone was his iron rose.
That woman had bequeathed for the rose to be placed on her grave forevermore.
As for Ostap, he began sentimentalizing and possibly died thereon on a road or under a wagon in a marketplace perhaps Amen!
On the other bank, Countess Branitsky's protected forest ascended a slope.
The sun couldn't penetrate through the dense greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally did an isolated ray cut diagonally through the thicket, revealing to us the astounding power of vegetation.
Like sparkly specks, little birds darted into this ray of light.
They chased each other with squeaks and plunged into the foliage as if it were green water.
I filled a bucket with water from the pond, tossed in some grass, and waited.
The red floats stood motionless in the water.
Then one of them began to shudder, creating slight ripples before suddenly diving or swiftly moving sideways.
My father would jerk the line, it became tight and bent into an arc on the walnut rod, and splashing and flapping began above the misty surface of the pond.
Water fanned out rocking lilies; water beetle hurriedly ran away in all directions, and finally a struggling golden glow appeared from within the mysterious depths.
It was impossible to make out what it was until my father dragged a heavy crucian carp onto crushed grass onto shore.
It lay on its side catching its breath while fluttering its fins;
an astonishing smell of an underwater kingdom came from its scales.
Yasha was counting seconds to himself.
We knew that it took seven minutes to walk from Sturdza Lane to Landesman's sanatorium.
In the sanatorium, behind a tall fence and iron gates, we always felt completely safe, especially if we didn't light any incense burners.
When we were passing a gateway, Yasha stumbled.
Later when we recalled the incident in Sturdza Lane, Yasha claimed that whenever you want to do something impeccably, some slight thing always interrupts you.
I myself thought that all this was due to Yasha's unbearable gait but stayed silent not wanting to upset him.
We stealthily walked down the alley.
I suggested we should walk on the side with the gateway, listen carefully before reaching it, then quickly and silently rush past.
The calculation, to my mind, was mathematically precise.
If there were people in the gateway, they could overlook us.
However, if we were to walk opposite from the gateway side, they might spot us from afar.

I calculated that in the latter scenario we would be walking towards or rather be in view of those hiding in a dangerous backstreet five times longer and hence there's likely a five times greater chance of being noticed.
In the morning I would wake up to the hot sun beating against the white walls.
Red and yellow hollyhocks swayed outside the open window.
Along with them, a nasturtium flower would peek into the room; a furry bee sat in it.
I would watch, still, as it angrily backed out and extracted itself from the tight blossom.
Light streaks ran endlessly across the ceiling, gentle waves reflecting off of the river.
The river was roaring right next door.
